MESSAGE:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest three things to do in Lisbon in the evening
2. Explain how to say 'thank you' in Portuguese and whether it varies by speaker
3. Say whether tipping is expected in Lisbon restaurants
4. Determine whether a 56 x 36 x 23 cm, 9 kg bag meets the carry-on limit  KEY: Missing datum: the airline (and fare type) is not stated, and carry-on size/weight limits vary by airline and fare, so this cannot be confirmed. Should ask which airline/fare and illustrate: under a common 55 x 40 x 20 cm limit the bag fails (56 > 55 length, 23 > 20 depth); under a 56 x 45 x 25 cm limit it fits; weight limits range roughly 7-10 kg, so 9 kg may exceed a 7 or 8 kg limit.
5. Recommend rolling vs folding shirts
6. Write a short out-of-office message
7. Suggest a luggage tag colour

ANSWER:
Here's everything in order, with return-journey tips at the end.

## Three things for a free evening in Lisbon

1. **Sunset at a miradouro (viewpoint).** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte and Miradouro de Santa Catarina both have wide views over the city and the river. Go about half an hour before sunset.
2. **Dinner and fado in Alfama or Mouraria.** Fado is Portugal's traditional music, sung in small restaurants and taverns. Book ahead if you can, and expect people to stay quiet during the songs.
3. **Wander Bairro Alto and Príncipe Real.** Bairro Alto fills up with small bars and people spilling into the streets later in the evening. Príncipe Real, next to it, is calmer and good for dinner. If you want something easy after meetings, the Time Out Market at Cais do Sodré has lots of food stalls under one roof.

## Saying thank you

- **Obrigado** if you're a man.
- **Obrigada** if you're a woman.

It depends on **who is speaking**, not who you're thanking. Add **muito** for "thank you very much": muito obrigado / muito obrigada.

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US, and service usually isn't added to the bill. In sit-down restaurants, people often round up or leave around **5–10% for good service**. In cafés, leaving small change is common. Nobody will mind if you don't tip.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

It depends on your airline and fare, and your bag is right on the edge of several common limits:

| Common cabin bag limit | Your bag (56 × 36 × 23 cm, 9 kg) |
|---|---|
| **55 × 40 × 20 cm, often 8 kg**, typical for many European full-service airlines | ❌ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep, and possibly 1 kg over |
| **56 × 45 × 25 cm**, with more generous weight limits, used by some airlines and larger cabin-bag options | ✅ fits |

Check your airline's current limits for your exact fare. Some basic economy fares include only a small under-seat bag. If you tell me the airline, I can tell you what to look for. If the weight limit is 8 kg, wearing your heaviest shoes and jacket on the plane usually solves it.

## Packing work shirts: fold

**Fold work shirts, and roll everything else.** Rolling tends to crease collars and leave tube-shaped wrinkles in crisp cotton. Fold shirts flat with collars buttoned, or use a packing folder.

Roll T-shirts, knitwear and casual clothes; they take up less space that way. When you arrive, hang the shirts in the bathroom while you shower and the steam will drop most creases. Most business hotels can also lend you an iron.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] and will have limited access to email during that time. I'll reply as soon as I can after I'm back on [date]. If your message is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

## Luggage tag colour

Go for something **bright and uncommon**, such as neon orange, lime green or hot pink. Most bags are black, grey or navy, and red and blue tags are common.

A tag still matters when you travel carry-on only. On full flights, cabin bags are often checked at the gate. If yours is, a bright tag helps you spot it, and make sure your name and phone number are inside the bag as well as on the tag.

## Making the Friday return less stressful

- **Pack on Friday morning**, before meetings, and either bring the bag with you or check whether the hotel will store it. Then go straight from your last meeting to the airport.
- **Check in online in advance** and keep your boarding pass on your phone. With carry-on only, you can go straight to security.
- **Allow plenty of time at Lisbon airport.** Security queues can be long on Friday evenings, so aim for at least two hours before departure. A taxi or ride-share from the centre usually takes 20–30 minutes without traffic. The metro's red line runs directly to the airport and avoids Friday traffic.
- **Keep your liquids bag and laptop at the top of your bag** for a quick pass through security.
- **Put a small "essentials" pouch in your jacket or personal bag:** phone charger, medication, keys and documents. If your cabin bag ends up gate-checked, those stay with you.

Enjoy Lisbon. It's a great city for a first visit.
